verdict.summary: A GitHub OAuth app works for any GitHub user as soon as you register it. GitHub does not review the app or its scopes. The main friction comes from organizations that restrict OAuth apps: an org owner has to approve your app before it can reach that org's resources. Review only applies if you choose to list on GitHub Marketplace.
verdict.hands_on_effort: 15-30 min (add 1-2 days if you build an optional Marketplace listing)
verdict.approval_wait: none for public use. Optional Marketplace listing: 2-6 weeks (community reports)

gates.name: Registered OAuth app (owner use)
gates.unlocks: You connect your own GitHub account through your own client ID and Composio's callback.
limits: Up to 100 OAuth apps per user or organization
Up to 10 callback URLs per app
Expire user access tokens is on by default: access tokens last 8 hours, refresh tokens 6 months without use

gates.name: Any GitHub user, with org approval where required (no test-user allowlist)
gates.unlocks: Teammates or invited users authorize the same app. GitHub has no separate test mode. Users in orgs with OAuth app access restrictions need an org owner to approve the app before it can reach that org's resources.
limits: OAuth app access restrictions are on by default for new orgs. Until an owner approves the app, it gets no API access to private org resources, receives no hooks from private org repos, and is blocked from privileged create/update/delete actions on public org resources
Org owners decide whether members, outside collaborators, both or neither can request approval
Re-authorization is required if the app signs in the same user more than 10 times in an hour
Requests made with a user token count against that user's 5,000/hour REST limit
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate. Org access waits on each org owner's approval.

gates.name: Public use (optional GitHub Marketplace listing)
gates.unlocks: Any GitHub user can authorize the app without any review. A Marketplace listing only adds discoverability and billing, and it is reviewed.
limits: 2,000 access token requests per hour per OAuth app. Going over temporarily blocks new tokens
Marketplace: privacy policy, support link, logo, screenshots and a pricing plan are required. The app must do more than authentication and must be publicly available
Paid Marketplace plans need a verified-publisher org and at least 200 users for an OAuth app
Only organization owners can submit listings for org-owned apps
gates.time_to_reach: Immediate for public use. Marketplace review is about 2-6 weeks (community reports; GitHub publishes no SLA).

steps.title: Decide whether a personal account or an org owns the app
steps.detail: You can register the app under your personal account or under any organization where you are an admin. If you might sell through Marketplace later, register it under an organization: paid listings need an org that is a verified publisher, and personal apps would have to be transferred.
gotchas: Each user or org can own at most 100 OAuth apps.

steps.title: Open the OAuth app registration form
steps.detail: Sign in to github.com and go to Settings > Developer settings > OAuth apps > New OAuth App. For your first app the button reads Register a new application. For an org-owned app, start from the organization's settings.
gotchas: Developer settings is only visible when you are signed in.

steps.title: Fill in the application name, homepage URL and description
steps.detail: An agent can draft the Application name, Homepage URL and optional Application description. You then paste them in. Users see these on the authorization screen.
gotchas: Only enter information you are happy to make public.

steps.title: Set the Authorization callback URL
steps.detail: In Authorization callback URL, paste the exact callback URL shown in your Composio auth config. You can add up to 10 callback URLs. If a request has no redirect_uri, GitHub uses the first one listed.

values.label: Redirect URI
values.value: Composio callback URL (see the Composio callout on this page)

gotchas: Apps with only one redirect URI have legacy wildcard matching turned on. Turn it off if you don't need it, because it can be abused when the target site hosts user content.

steps.title: Choose token expiry and device flow settings, then register
steps.detail: Expire user access tokens is checked by default: access tokens last 8 hours, and refresh tokens last 6 months without use. Leave it on only if your Composio setup refreshes tokens; otherwise uncheck it. Check Enable Device Flow only if you need headless or CLI sign-in. Then click Register application.
gotchas: Turning on expiring tokens later only affects new tokens. Existing tokens stay long-lived until users sign in again.
Each refresh returns a new refresh token, so store the new one every time.

steps.title: Copy the client credentials into a Composio auth config
steps.detail: On the new app's page, copy the Client ID and a client secret. In Composio, create a GitHub (toolkit 'github') auth config that uses your own OAuth credentials. Request only the scopes your agent needs; don't copy Composio's full default list.
gotchas: The repo scope gives full read/write access to public and private repos. workflow lets the app change GitHub Actions workflow files.

steps.title: Run a test authorization with your own account
steps.detail: Start a connection from Composio, approve the GitHub consent screen and check that a token comes back and an API call works. The authorization code expires after 10 minutes. If you use PKCE, only S256 is accepted.

steps.title: Get the app approved in organizations that restrict OAuth apps
steps.detail: If a user's org has OAuth app access restrictions (on by default for new orgs), the user requests approval during sign-in. An org owner then approves it under Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy > Review > Grant access.
steps.est_time: Minutes per org (depends on the owner)
gotchas: Without approval, the app silently has no access to private org repos, even though the user's authorization succeeds.
An org can block outside collaborators from requesting approval.

steps.title: Roll out to users and watch rate limits
steps.detail: Any GitHub user can now connect, and no GitHub review is needed. Monitor the app-wide limit of 2,000 token requests per hour, the per-user sign-in throttle, and the 5,000 requests/hour REST limit per user (15,000 for apps owned by GitHub Enterprise Cloud orgs).

steps.title: (Optional) Draft a Marketplace listing
steps.detail: Only do this if you want to be listed on Marketplace. An agent can draft the description, privacy policy, support, Terms and Status links, logo, feature card, screenshots and a pricing plan. Paid plans also need webhooks for plan changes and cancellations.
gotchas: The app must do more than authentication and must be publicly available, not beta or invite-only.

steps.title: (Optional) Accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement and submit
steps.detail: Accept the Marketplace Developer Agreement and click Submit for review on the listing's Overview page. For org-owned apps, only an organization owner can submit.
gotchas: Community reports say you need a verified public email and two-factor authentication.
Paid listings for OAuth apps need a verified-publisher org and at least 200 users.

steps.title: (Optional) Wait for Marketplace review
steps.detail: GitHub publishes no review SLA. Community reports put it at 2-6 weeks, and longer if reviewers have questions about security, OAuth or billing. If there is no update after about 3 weeks, open a Marketplace support ticket.

requirements.item: GitHub account (admin rights if the app is org-owned)
requirements.detail: You can register OAuth apps under your personal account or under orgs where you are an admin.

requirements.item: Public app name, homepage URL and callback URL
requirements.detail: Name and homepage are required, and users see them. Up to 10 callback URLs are allowed.

requirements.item: Org owner approval for restricted orgs
requirements.detail: Orgs with OAuth app access restrictions must approve the app before it can reach their private resources.
Publisher contact info, description, pricing plan, privacy policy link, support link or email, Terms and Status links, logo, feature card and screenshots.

requirements.item: Verified publisher org and 200+ users (paid Marketplace only)
requirements.detail: Required only for paid Marketplace plans. Free listings need just the general requirements.

requirements.item: Marketplace Developer Agreement, 2FA and verified public email (optional listing)
requirements.detail: The agreement is in official docs. The 2FA and verified email requirements come from community reports.

scopes.effect: Full read/write access to public and private repos, plus org projects, invitations, team memberships and webhooks. GitHub does not tier scopes or review them for OAuth apps.
Lets the app add and update GitHub Actions workflow files. It is in Composio's default list, so drop it unless your agent needs it.
High-privilege scopes (full org management, repo deletion). They need no review, but users see them on the consent screen and can remove them.
Gets an expiring access token plus a refresh token for that sign-in, even if the app is not set to expire tokens.

blockers.symptom: A user connects successfully, but API calls to their org's private repos fail or return nothing.
blockers.cause: The org has OAuth app access restrictions enabled (on by default for new orgs), and nobody has approved your app.
blockers.fix: Have the user request approval. An org owner then approves it under Settings > Third-party Access > OAuth app policy > Review > Grant access.

blockers.symptom: Connections stop working after about 8 hours.
blockers.cause: Expire user access tokens is on by default for new apps, and refresh isn't being handled.
blockers.fix: Make sure refresh tokens are used and stored, or uncheck Expire user access tokens in the app settings.

blockers.symptom: New sign-ins fail for every user for a while.
blockers.cause: The app went over 2,000 access token requests per hour.
blockers.fix: Cut down on token churn (reuse tokens, don't re-authorize repeatedly). For scale, consider a GitHub App or ask GitHub for a per-app rate-limit increase.

blockers.symptom: A user is asked to re-authorize the app unexpectedly.
blockers.cause: The app signed in the same user 10 times within an hour.
blockers.fix: Reuse the user's existing token instead of starting a new OAuth flow.

blockers.symptom: The Marketplace section doesn't appear, or the listing sits in review for weeks.
blockers.cause: The section only shows if the app can be installed by any user or org. Reviews have no SLA and slow down when reviewers have questions about security, OAuth or billing.
blockers.fix: Check the app's install setting. If there is no update after about 3 weeks, open a Marketplace support ticket.

composio.note: Use Composio's managed GitHub OAuth app while prototyping. Switch to your own OAuth app when you want your own name on the consent screen, your own client ID and token-request rate-limit budget, or narrower scopes than Composio's defaults (which include repo, user and workflow). Your own app needs no GitHub review, so switching takes about 15 minutes. GitHub recommends GitHub Apps for new integrations, because OAuth apps have lower limits that don't scale.

open_questions: Does Composio's GitHub integration handle the refresh-token flow for expiring (8-hour) tokens? If not, uncheck Expire user access tokens.
The findings don't describe the exact UI steps for generating a client secret on the app page. Check this when you create the app.
Is there really no review for high-privilege scopes (admin:org, delete_repo)? The scope page shows no review tier; confirm with GitHub support if it matters.
No GitHub-published user or install cap for unreviewed OAuth apps was found. Org-level approval is the only documented gate.
The steps for publisher verification for organizations were not checked.
Marketplace review timing comes only from community reports; GitHub publishes no SLA.
The signed-in registration form was not directly observed. Field labels come from GitHub's docs.
Consider whether a GitHub App (fine-grained permissions, limits that scale) suits you better than an OAuth app. GitHub recommends it, and this guide doesn't cover it.
